summary: The transition tables correctly increment every supported 12-bit integer and run the two busy-beaver examples. The busy-beaver machines leave four and six ones. This is a finite, bounded demonstration of Turing’s tape model.

claims.how: The head, states, write actions, and moves illustrate his model; the universal-computation claim presumes enough tape and time.

sources.title: On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem
sources.publisher: Alan Turing, 1936; University of Virginia copy
sources.says: Turing defines computation using a tape, scanned symbols, states, and transition rules, and describes a universal machine.

claims.claim: The add-one program implements binary carry.
claims.how: Every integer from 0 through 4095 produces its independently calculated increment; 1011 becomes 1100.

claims.claim: The two- and three-state busy beavers write four and six ones.
claims.how: Independent rule traces agree with all writes, moves, states, halts, and final tapes, taking six and 13 transitions respectively.

sources.title: Busy beaver research
sources.says: The maximum numbers of ones for two and three states are four and six. The longest three-state runtime is 21 steps.

claims.note: Six ones is a maximum-output claim; this three-state table is not the 21-step maximum-runtime champion.

claims.claim: The tape picture is a bounded illustration.
claims.how: The input parser caps the bit count and the interpreter caps the transition count; this is not an implementation with unlimited tape and time.

simplified: Input is at most 12 bits and runs stop after 60 transitions. A 13th overflow bit can lie outside the visible strip. The three-state six-one example runs in 13 steps; the separate maximum-runtime record is 21, not 13.
